title: CLAT — Logical Reasoning | Criminal Law Basics
description: Subject-wise test on Criminal Law Basics (Logical Reasoning) for CLAT. 30Q.
subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Ramesh decided to break into an empty warehouse to steal copper wires. Unknown to Ramesh, an unhoused person, Shyam, was sleeping inside covered under a pile of discarded burlap sacks. While using a gas-cutter to breach an iron cabinet, a stray spark ignited the burlap sacks, causing Shyam's death due to asphyxiation. Ramesh is charged with murder, which requires the intention to cause death or knowledge that the act is likely to cause death. Applying the passage, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Ramesh is liable for murder because he was committing an unlawful act of theft, and all unintended harms are absorbed into his unlawful purpose.
options.explanation: This is incorrect because mens rea is required for murder; unlawful intent for theft does not automatically transfer to homicide without specific intent or knowledge regarding the death.

options.text: Ramesh is not liable for murder because he neither desired Shyam’s death nor had the requisite knowledge of Shyam’s presence inside the warehouse.
options.explanation: Correct. Ramesh lacked the specific intention or knowledge of Shyam's presence, which are necessary elements for the mens rea of murder.

options.text: Ramesh is liable under the doctrine of transferred malice since his unlawful intention to steal transfers to the resulting homicide.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Transferred malice applies when intent to harm one person transfers to another person, not when intent to commit a property crime transfers to a homicide.

options.text: Ramesh is strictly liable because the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea does not apply to property crimes resulting in bodily injury.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The maxim applies generally; strict liability is not the standard for murder, which requires mens rea.

questions.explanation: Under the passage, criminal liability requires the simultaneous concurrence of actus reus and the prescribed mens rea (intention or knowledge). Ramesh broke into what he believed was an empty warehouse; he did not foresee or desire Shyam's death, nor did he possess awareness (knowledge) of Shyam's presence under the sacks. Transferred malice requires intending a crime against one person and harming another, not an intention directed purely at property transferring into homicide. Hence, Ramesh lacks the requisite mens rea for murder.
questions.hint: Consider whether Ramesh had the specific mental state (intention or knowledge) required for murder regarding the victim's presence.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Vikram intends to assassinate Mohan by shooting him at a crowded rally. Vikram aims carefully at Mohan’s chest and fires. However, at the exact moment the bullet is discharged, Mohan bends down to tie his shoelace, and the bullet strikes and kills Sohan, a bystander standing directly behind Mohan. Vikram argues that he cannot be convicted of murdering Sohan because he had no personal grievance, animus, or plan to harm Sohan. Decide based on the passage.

options.text: Vikram cannot be convicted of murdering Sohan because the actus reus did not correspond to his subjective intention towards Sohan.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The doctrine of transferred malice bridges the gap between the intended victim and the actual victim.

options.text: Vikram can only be convicted of causing death by negligence because hitting Sohan was an unintended accident.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Vikram had the intent to kill (Mohan), which transfers to Sohan, making it murder, not just negligence.

options.text: Vikram is liable for the murder of Sohan under the doctrine of transferred malice, as his intention to kill Mohan transfers to Sohan.
options.explanation: Correct. The intention to kill the intended target transfers to the actual victim under the doctrine of transferred malice.

options.text: Vikram is not liable because a pre-arranged plan against the actual victim is a mandatory prerequisite for homicide.
options.explanation: Incorrect. There is no requirement for a pre-arranged plan against the specific actual victim if transferred malice applies.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly defines the doctrine of transferred malice: if a person intends to commit an offence against one person and inadvertently causes a similar harm to an unintended victim, the law transfers the blameworthy intention to the actual victim, and the accused cannot plead an absence of specific animus toward the unintended target. Vikram intended to kill Mohan and caused the death of Sohan; hence, his intention transfers.
questions.hint: Recall the definition of transferred malice provided in the passage regarding unintended victims.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Arun, Tarun, and Varun arrive at a local shop. Arun and Tarun have previously agreed to beat up the shopkeeper, Dev, to avenge an insult. Varun accompanies them merely to watch the altercation and stands at the shop entrance without uttering a word, blocking the door, or issuing threats. During the assault, Arun and Tarun strike Dev with iron rods, fracturing his skull. The prosecution charges all three, including Varun, under joint liability for common intention. Is Varun liable?

options.text: Yes, because Varun’s presence at the scene proves that he shared the common intention to beat Dev.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Mere presence without prior concert or participation is insufficient for joint liability.

options.text: No, because mere passive presence without prior concert or physical participation does not attract joint liability under common intention.
options.explanation: Correct. Varun lacked both the prior agreement (concert) and the physical participation required for joint liability.

options.text: Yes, because any companion accompanying assailants is conclusively presumed to act in furtherance of a common design.
options.explanation: Incorrect. There is no conclusive presumption of common design based solely on companionship.

options.text: No, because common intention requires that every participant must personally wield a weapon and strike the victim.
options.explanation: Incorrect. While Varun is not liable, the reason is not that everyone must wield a weapon, but that he lacked concert and participation.

questions.explanation: According to the passage, to invoke joint liability under common intention, two essential conditions must be fulfilled: "first, there must be a prior concert—a pre-arranged plan or meeting of minds... and second, there must be physical participation in some form in the commission of the offence." Varun merely accompanied them to watch and stood at the entrance without participating or being part of the prior concert. Thus, he cannot be held liable under common intention.
questions.hint: Check if Varun met the two conditions for joint liability: prior concert and physical participation.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Karan and Arjun independently harbor a deep grudge against Bhiku. Neither knows of the other’s hostility or intentions. On Monday evening, both coincidentally spot Bhiku walking along a secluded alley. Acting purely on his own initiative, Karan rushes forward and stabs Bhiku in the stomach. Simultaneously, Arjun picks up a stone from the ground and hurls it at Bhiku, fracturing his arm. Bhiku survives. The prosecution seeks to hold Karan and Arjun jointly liable for both the stab wound and the fractured arm on grounds of common intention. Applying the passage, will the prosecution succeed?

options.text: No, because Karan and Arjun acted with "similar intention" rather than "common intention," lacking a prior concert or shared design.
options.explanation: Correct. They acted independently without a shared plan, which constitutes similar intention, not common intention.

options.text: Yes, because a common intention arose spontaneously on the spot the moment both attacked Bhiku at the exact same time.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Simultaneous independent actions do not create a common intention without a prior or spontaneous meeting of minds.

options.text: Yes, because both intended to cause bodily harm to the same individual in the course of the same transaction.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sharing the same objective is not enough; a shared design or concert is required.

options.text: No, because joint liability can only apply if the victim actually dies as a consequence of the joint acts.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Joint liability is not contingent on the victim's death.

questions.explanation: The passage notes: "Several individuals independently harboring the same objective without a shared design or mutual understanding do not act in furtherance of a common intention, and each remains liable solely for his own distinct act." Karan and Arjun had no meeting of minds or shared design; they acted independently out of coincidence, which is a textbook case of "similar intention," not "common intention."
questions.hint: Distinguish between 'common intention' and 'similar intention' as defined in the passage.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Deepak, Farhan, and Gurpreet plan an unarmed house burglary. Their explicit, agreed-upon pact is that if any occupant wakes up, they will immediately flee without engaging in violence. During the burglary, the homeowner wakes up and catches Farhan by the collar. While Deepak and Gurpreet turn to flee as planned, Farhan suddenly pulls an unlicensed pistol from his pocket—which he had concealed without the knowledge of Deepak or Gurpreet—and shoots the homeowner dead. Are Deepak and Gurpreet jointly liable for the homeowner's murder?

options.text: Yes, because all three participated in the unlawful enterprise of burglary, and are jointly responsible for any consequence arising from it.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Liability is limited to acts within the scope of the common intention; Farhan's act was extraneous.

options.text: Yes, because physical presence at the scene of an armed crime makes all participants equally culpable for murder.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Presence alone does not create liability for acts outside the scope of the conspiracy.

options.text: No, because Farhan’s act of shooting was an unexpected, extraneous act outside the scope of their pre-arranged, unarmed plan.
options.explanation: Correct. Farhan's use of a concealed weapon was outside the scope of the agreed unarmed plan, so others are not liable.

options.text: No, because joint liability applies exclusively to pre-planned homicides and never to property offences.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Joint liability can apply to property offences if the conditions are met, but here it fails due to the extraneous nature of the act.

questions.explanation: The passage clearly provides: "Finally, if one co-conspirator embarks on an unexpected, totally extraneous venture entirely outside the contemplated scope of the pre-arranged plan, other participants cannot be held vicariously liable for that specific unauthorized act." Here, the agreed plan was explicitly unarmed and non-violent with an agreement to flee; Farhan's concealed firearm and lethal shooting were completely outside the scope of the pre-arranged design.
questions.hint: Consider whether Farhan's act was within the scope of the pre-arranged plan.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Aman receives an anonymous handwritten letter on Monday morning stating: "I know you live alone. On Friday night at 11:00 PM, I will come to your house and break your legs." The police station is situated 500 meters from Aman’s house. Instead of informing the police, Aman purchases a shotgun. On Friday night, when a masked trespasser enters his lawn carrying an iron rod, Aman shoots him from his balcony, killing him. Aman pleads the right of private defence. Will his defence succeed?

options.text: Yes, because a person is entitled to defend their home against nocturnal trespassers armed with deadly weapons.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The right is barred because he had time to seek police help.

options.text: Yes, because the apprehension of bodily harm commenced on Monday upon reading the threatening letter.
options.explanation: Incorrect. While apprehension started earlier, the availability of police protection negates the right.

options.text: No, because Aman had ample time and opportunity between Monday and Friday to seek the protection of public authorities.
options.explanation: Correct. The right of private defence is not available when there is reasonable time to seek police protection.

options.text: No, because the right of private defence never permits causing the death of a trespasser under any circumstance.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Death can be justified in private defence under specific conditions (e.g., apprehension of death/grievous hurt), but here the bar is the availability of police.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly lays down: "Third, no right of private defence exists where there is reasonable opportunity and time to seek recourse to the protection of public authorities, such as the police." Aman had five days (Monday to Friday) and lived only 500 meters from a police station, yet deliberately chose not to inform the authorities. Therefore, the right of private defence is excluded.
questions.hint: Check if Aman had a reasonable opportunity to seek police protection.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Kavita is walking down an isolated street when an unarmed man, Bunty, blocks her path, uses abusive language, and attempts to snatch her handbag containing ₹500. Bunty makes no gesture suggesting an intention to cause grievous hurt or death. Kavita pulls out an unlicensed revolver and shoots Bunty through the heart, killing him instantly. She claims private defence of property and body. Which of the following correctly assesses Kavita’s liability under the passage?

options.text: Kavita is fully protected because the right of private defence allows the protection of one's property and person against any unlawful restraint.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The force used must be proportionate to the threat.

options.text: Kavita is protected because an isolated street leaves no time to contact public authorities.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Even if police were unavailable, the force used was disproportionate to the threat of a simple snatch.

options.text: Kavita exceeded her right of private defence because causing death is disproportionate and only justifiable where there is a reasonable apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, or kidnapping.
options.explanation: Correct. The threat did not justify lethal force, making the act disproportionate.

options.text: Option D

questions.explanation: According to the passage, the right of private defence is subject to proportionality and "does not extend to the infliction of more harm than is reasonably necessary." Furthermore, "Causing death in the exercise of private defence is justifiable only if the assailant's act reasonably causes an apprehension that death, grievous hurt, rape, or kidnapping will otherwise be the inevitable consequence." An unarmed purse-snatcher using abusive words did not create an apprehension of death or grievous hurt; thus, shooting him dead was a disproportionate use of force exceeding the right.
questions.hint: Assess the proportionality of the defensive force used relative to the threat posed.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Raman was returning home at night carrying an antique porcelain vase. Suman, an unarmed teenager, suddenly jumped out from behind a bush and shouted aggressively, "Give me your watch, or I'll punch you!" Raman, terrified of losing his watch, immediately pulled out a licensed firearm and shot Suman in the chest, killing him instantly. Applying the principles in the passage, Raman is:

options.text: Protected by the right of private defence, as Suman was an unlawful aggressor attempting robbery.
options.explanation: While Suman was an aggressor, the response was disproportionate to the threat of simple hurt.

options.text: Protected by the right of private defence, because the right commences the moment an apprehension of an offence arises.
options.explanation: The right commences, but it is limited by proportionality. Lethal force is not justified for a threat of simple hurt.

options.text: Liable for causing Suman's death, because his response was disproportionate and the threat did not warrant lethal force.
options.explanation: The threat was of simple hurt (a punch), so causing death exceeds the legitimate bounds of the right of private defence.

options.text: Liable only if Suman did not actually possess the physical strength to inflict a severe punch.
options.explanation: The liability stems from the disproportionality of the response to the nature of the threat, not the physical strength of the aggressor.

questions.explanation: The right of private defence is governed by proportionality. Causing death is restricted to situations with a reasonable apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, or kidnapping. Suman's threat of a punch constitutes simple hurt, making lethal force disproportionate.
questions.hint: Consider the proportionality of the response to the threat.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Kabir noticed a thief, Suraj, sneaking out of his farmhouse carrying Kabir's expensive stereo system. Suraj dropped the stereo, raised his hands, and began running away across an open field. Kabir picked up his hunting rifle, aimed at the fleeing Suraj, and shot him in the leg to prevent him from escaping. Which of the following is true regarding Kabir’s actions?

options.text: Kabir acted legally because the right of private defence extends to protecting one's property until the thief is apprehended.
options.explanation: The right does not extend to pursuit after the threat has ended and the property has been abandoned.

options.text: Kabir acted unlawfully because the right of private defence ceased once Suraj abandoned the property and fled.
options.explanation: The apprehension of danger to property ended when Suraj dropped the stereo and fled, so the right to use force ceased.

options.text: Kabir acted legally because he merely shot Suraj in the leg rather than aiming to kill him.
options.explanation: The right itself had ceased, so any use of force was unlawful regardless of the severity of the injury.

options.text: Kabir acted unlawfully only because firearms can never be used under the right of private defence of property.
options.explanation: The passage does not categorically ban firearms; the issue is the cessation of the right due to the end of the threat.

questions.explanation: The right of private defence continues only as long as the apprehension of danger persists. Once Suraj dropped the property and fled, the threat ceased, making the subsequent shooting unlawful.
questions.hint: When does the right of private defence cease?
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Inspector Roy, dressed in regular civilian clothes without any uniform, insignia, or badge, approached Dev in an isolated alley, drew a knife, and grabbed Dev's shoulder to arrest him under a secret, valid warrant. Dev, having no idea Roy was a police officer and believing he was being mugged with a deadly weapon, struck Roy forcefully with a metal rod, fracturing Roy’s skull. Dev is:

options.text: Entitled to claim the right of private defence, because Roy’s actions created a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
options.explanation: Dev had a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt due to Roy's appearance and actions, justifying the defensive strike.

options.text: Not entitled to claim private defence, because Roy was a public servant acting pursuant to a valid legal warrant.
options.explanation: The right exists against public servants if their act causes a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

options.text: Not entitled to claim private defence, because Dev had an absolute duty to verify the identity of an armed assailant.
options.explanation: There is no such absolute duty in the context of immediate threat; the standard is reasonable apprehension.

options.text: Entitled to claim private defence only if Roy actively declared an intent to kill Dev.
options.explanation: An explicit declaration of intent to kill is not required; reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt is sufficient.

questions.explanation: The right of private defence exists against public servants acting lawfully if their act causes a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. Roy's actions in plain clothes with a knife created such an apprehension.
questions.hint: Check the exception for public servants in the passage.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Tarun was severely beaten by a gang of three armed men who cornered him in a courtyard. Tarun managed to snatch a machete from one of the attackers, Tarik. Seeing Tarun armed, all three attackers turned and began frantically climbing over a high wall to escape. Tarun, enraged and bleeding, hacked Tarik’s legs as he was scaling the wall, causing Tarik to fall and die of blood loss. Can Tarun successfully invoke the right of private defence?

options.text: Yes, because Tarun had suffered grievous hurt immediately prior and the aggression originated from the deceased.
options.explanation: The right is not punitive; past aggression does not justify current harm once the threat has ended.

options.text: Yes, because a defender is not expected to modulate their response in the heat of a brutal assault.
options.explanation: The defender must cease using force once the threat has ended, even if they are still in the heat of the moment.

options.text: No, because the right of private defence is defensive, not retributive, and the apprehension had ended once the attackers were in retreat.
options.explanation: The attackers were fleeing, so the apprehension of danger had ceased. Attacking them was retributive, not defensive.

options.text: No, because one cannot claim private defence using a weapon that initially belonged to the aggressor.
options.explanation: The source of the weapon is irrelevant; the issue is the timing and nature of the response.

questions.explanation: The right of private defence is purely defensive and preventive, not punitive. Once the attackers were retreating, the apprehension of danger ceased, so attacking them was retributive.
questions.hint: Is the right of private defence punitive?
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: A local municipal corporation passed an environmental regulation stating: "Whoever discharges untreated industrial effluents into the city river shall be punished with imprisonment up to one year or a fine." GreenChem Ltd. installed state-of-the-art filtration units and hired top environmental auditors who certified the discharge as completely purified water. However, due to an unprecedented subterranean seismic tremor, a hidden valve cracked, releasing untreated chemical effluents into the river. If the prosecution argues that the regulation creates a "strict liability offence", what is the legal outcome?

options.text: GreenChem is liable, as strict liability attaches upon the occurrence of the prohibited physical act regardless of the absence of mens rea.
options.explanation: Strict liability means the mental state is irrelevant; the act itself creates liability.

options.text: GreenChem is not liable, because the ancient maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea overrides all modern statutory texts.
options.explanation: The maxim is overridden when a statute explicitly creates a strict liability offence.

options.text: GreenChem is not liable, because the company took all reasonable precautions and did not intend the discharge.
options.explanation: Reasonable precautions and lack of intent are irrelevant in strict liability offences.

options.text: GreenChem is liable only if the prosecution proves that the company directors possessed reckless disregard of the seismic tremor.
options.explanation: Recklessness is a form of mens rea, which is not required for strict liability.

questions.explanation: In strict liability offences, liability attaches upon the occurrence of the prohibited physical act (actus reus) regardless of the absence of mens rea (mental state).
questions.hint: What is the effect of strict liability on mens rea?
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Rohan, a licensed truck driver, was driving at 40 km/h on a well-lit highway. Suddenly, a pedestrian wearing black clothes ran across the road outside of a designated crossing zone. Rohan swerved and applied brakes immediately, but hit the pedestrian, who died of head injuries. Rohan had neither intent to harm nor knowledge that a person would suddenly bolt across. Rohan’s act:

options.text: Amounts to murder, because operating heavy motor vehicles is an inherently imminently dangerous activity.
options.explanation: Operating a vehicle is not inherently imminently dangerous in the legal sense if reasonable care is exercised.

options.text: Amounts to culpable homicide, because causing death on public roads is presumed to be accompanied by knowledge.
options.explanation: There is no such presumption; knowledge must be proven.

options.text: Is a rash and negligent act causing death, as every fatal vehicular collision attracts criminal negligence.
options.explanation: Not every fatal collision is negligent; reasonable care was exercised here.

options.text: Does not amount to culpable homicide or murder, and he is not liable if he exercised the reasonable care expected of a driver.
options.explanation: Rohan lacked intent/knowledge and exercised reasonable care, so he is not liable for culpable homicide or negligence.

questions.explanation: Rohan lacked the intention or knowledge required for culpable homicide. Since he exercised reasonable care, it is not even a rash or negligent act.
questions.hint: What elements are required for culpable homicide?
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Vikas discovered that his business partner, Alok, had embezzled their firm's funds. Vikas confronted Alok on Monday morning; Alok laughed, hurled filthy abuses at Vikas’s family, and spat on Vikas's face. Vikas walked away trembling in anger. On Wednesday evening—two days later—Vikas spotted Alok having coffee, walked up behind him with an iron rod, and struck him on the head, killing him. Vikas pleaded the exception of "Grave and Sudden Provocation". Will his plea succeed?

options.text: Yes, because spitting in someone's face and abusing their family constitutes grave provocation under any reasonable standard.
options.explanation: While the provocation may be grave, it was not sudden due to the time lapse.

options.text: No, because the lapse of two days provided sufficient time for a reasonable person’s passions to cool down, destroying the element of suddenness.
options.explanation: The two-day gap negates the 'sudden' nature of the provocation.

options.text: Yes, because financial embezzlement combined with verbal insults keeps provocation alive until satisfaction is obtained.
options.explanation: Provocation does not remain alive indefinitely; it must be sudden.

options.text: No, because the exception of provocation can only be claimed if the weapon used is bare hands, not an iron rod.
options.explanation: The type of weapon is not a condition for the provocation exception.

questions.explanation: The provocation must be sudden. A lapse of two days allows sufficient time for passions to cool, negating the element of suddenness.
questions.hint: How much time is allowed for the provocation to be considered 'sudden'?
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Mahesh, during a heated domestic squabble with his tenant Girish, picked up a heavy wooden mallet and struck Girish squarely on the temple with tremendous force. Medical experts testified in court that a blow of such force with that weapon to the human skull is objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Mahesh argued he did not harbour an explicit "intention to kill". Mahesh is guilty of:

options.text: Murder, because he intended to inflict a bodily injury that was objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
options.explanation: The intention to inflict an injury that is objectively sufficient to cause death meets the threshold for murder.

options.text: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, because he lacked the specific subjective intention to extinguish Girish's life.
options.explanation: Specific intention to kill is not required if the intended injury is objectively sufficient to cause death.

options.text: A rash and negligent act, because the blow was struck during an unexpected domestic squabble without premeditation.
options.explanation: The act was intentional, not rash or negligent.

options.text: Grievous hurt only, because the strike was a single blow with a household object.
options.explanation: The injury was objectively sufficient to cause death, elevating it to murder.

questions.explanation: Murder can be established if the offender intends to inflict a bodily injury that is objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, even without a specific intention to kill.
questions.hint: What is the threshold for murder regarding bodily injury?
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: In a charge of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, which of the following is the essential element that must be proved?

options.text: The victim was a public servant.
options.explanation: The status of the victim is not an essential element for the basic offence of murder under Section 302.

options.text: The accused had the intention to cause death.
options.explanation: Intention or knowledge to cause death is the core mens rea required for murder under Section 302.

options.text: The death occurred within the jurisdiction of India.
options.explanation: While jurisdiction is a procedural requirement, it is not the specific essential element defining the offence of murder itself in the context of the question's focus on the actus reus/mens rea.

options.text: The accused was previously convicted of a similar offence.
options.explanation: Prior conviction is not an element of the offence of murder.

questions.explanation: Section 302 requires that the accused had the intention (or knowledge) to cause death. The other factors are not essential for the offence of murder.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: A person is charged with attempt to commit theft under Section 379 of the IPC. Which statement correctly describes the mens-repa requirement for an attempt?

options.text: The accused must have actually taken the property.
options.explanation: If the property was actually taken, it would be completed theft, not attempt.

options.text: The accused must have performed an overt act beyond mere preparation.
options.explanation: Attempt requires an overt act that moves beyond the stage of preparation towards the commission of the offence.

options.text: The accused must have a prior conviction for theft.
options.explanation: Prior conviction is not a requirement for the offence of attempt.

options.text: The accused must have a motive to steal.
options.explanation: Motive is not a legal element of the offence; intent is the relevant mental state.

questions.explanation: For an attempt, the prosecution must prove an overt act that goes beyond preparation and shows a clear intent to commit the crime. Mere preparation is insufficient.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Raj, aged 22, voluntarily consumed large quantities of alcohol and, while heavily intoxicated, assaulted a stranger, causing grievous hurt. He claims intoxication as a defence. Which of the following is the correct legal position?

options.text: Intoxication completely absolves him of criminal liability.
options.explanation: Voluntary intoxication does not absolve liability for general intent offences.

options.text: Intoxication is a defence only if it negates the actus reus.
options.explanation: Intoxication affects the mental state (mens rea), not the physical act (actus reus).

options.text: Voluntary intoxication is not a defence to offences requiring mens rea such as grievous hurt.
options.explanation: For general intent offences like grievous hurt, voluntary intoxication is not a valid defence.

options.text: The court will treat him as a minor because of his impaired state.
options.explanation: Intoxication does not change the legal age or status of the accused.

questions.explanation: Under the IPC, voluntary intoxication is not a defence to offences that require mens rea (e.g., grievous hurt). It may be considered only for specific intent crimes, not for general intent offences like this.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: An 18-year-old male, with the victim’s consent, engages in sexual intercourse with a 10-year-old girl. Under Section 376(2) of the IPC, the accused is:

options.text: Acquitted because the victim gave consent.
options.explanation: Consent of a child below 12 is legally invalid.

options.text: Charged with rape only if the victim is below 12 years and the accused is above 18 years.
options.explanation: While the conditions are met, this option is phrased as a conditional statement rather than a direct legal conclusion of liability. Option C is the more direct and accurate statement of the legal position.

options.text: Liable for rape, as the victim is below 12 years, irrespective of consent.
options.explanation: The law presumes that a child below 12 cannot give valid consent, making the act rape regardless of any apparent consent.

options.text: Not liable because the accused is a minor.
options.explanation: The accused is 18 years old, which is an adult in the context of this specific provision.

questions.explanation: Section 376(2) makes it a rape if the victim is below 12 years, regardless of consent, and the offender is above 18 years. The consent of a minor is legally irrelevant.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: After being acquitted of a theft charge, Sameer is later charged with the same offence for the same conduct. Which constitutional principle prevents this second prosecution?

options.text: Right to equality.
options.explanation: Equality is not the specific principle preventing double prosecution.

options.text: Double jeopardy under Article 20(2) of the Constitution.
options.explanation: Article 20(2) explicitly protects against double jeopardy.

options.text: Right to life.
options.explanation: While related to fundamental rights, it is not the specific provision for double jeopardy.

options.text: Doctrine of pith and substance.
options.explanation: This doctrine relates to legislative competence, not criminal procedure.

questions.explanation: Article 20(2) guarantees that no person shall be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence, embodying the double jeopardy principle.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Maya, a shopkeeper, uses a firearm to ward off a thief who is attempting to steal goods worth ₹5,000. In doing so, she injures the thief severely. Which statement best reflects the law on private defence?

options.text: Private defence of property permits lethal force.
options.explanation: Lethal force is generally not permitted for the defence of property alone.

options.text: Lethal force is permissible only when there is a threat to life, not merely property.
options.explanation: The use of force must be proportionate; lethal force is reserved for threats to life or personal safety.

options.text: The shopkeeper can be charged with murder irrespective of the thief’s intent.
options.explanation: The context of private defence is relevant to the charge and potential acquittal.

options.text: The defence is unavailable because the thief was unarmed.
options.explanation: The availability of defence depends on the threat posed, not just whether the thief was armed.

questions.explanation: The right of private defence allows only as much force as is necessary to repel the threat. Lethal force is justified only if there is a threat to life, not merely to protect property.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: In a criminal trial, the prosecution fails to produce any direct evidence linking the accused to the crime, but the defence also offers no evidence. What is the legal status of the accused?

options.text: The accused is automatically convicted under the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.
options.explanation: Res ipsa loquitur is a civil law concept and does not apply to criminal conviction.

options.text: The accused is presumed innocent and must be acquitted due to lack of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
options.explanation: The burden of proof lies with the prosecution; failure to prove guilt results in acquittal.

options.text: The court may convict based on circumstantial evidence alone.
options.explanation: The question states the prosecution failed to produce *any* direct evidence, implying a lack of sufficient evidence overall to meet the standard of proof.

options.text: The burden shifts to the accused to prove innocence.
options.explanation: The burden of proof remains with the prosecution in criminal cases.

questions.explanation: The presumption of innocence is a cornerstone of criminal law; the prosecution bears the burden of proof. Without proof, the accused must be acquitted.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Rahul, in a sudden fight, stabs his neighbour, causing death. He claims “grave and sudden provocation” as a defence. The prosecution charges him under Section 307 (attempt to murder) and Section 302 (murder). Considering the facts, which charge is most appropriate?

options.text: Only Section 307, because the provocation negates the intention to kill.
options.explanation: Provocation does not negate the act of causing death, nor does it reduce the offence to attempt.

options.text: Both sections, as the court can convict under both simultaneously.
options.explanation: One cannot be convicted of both murder and attempt to murder for the same act.

options.text: Section 302, because the provocation does not reduce the offence to mere attempt.
options.explanation: Since death occurred, the charge is for the completed offence. Provocation might mitigate the sentence or change the section to 304, but it does not make it an attempt.

options.text: Neither, as provocation makes the act a civil wrong.
options.explanation: Provocation does not decriminalize the act of causing death.

questions.explanation: “Grave and sudden provocation” may reduce a murder charge to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304, but it does not reduce the offence to mere attempt. Since death resulted, the appropriate charge is murder under Section 302; the attempt charge is redundant.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: A defendant is convicted of three offences: Offence A: 2 years imprisonment (simple imprisonment). Offence B: 3 years imprisonment (simple imprisonment). Offence C: 1 year imprisonment (simple imprisonment). The court orders consecutive sentences for A and B, and concurrent sentencing for C with B. What is the total period of imprisonment? Show calculations.

options.text: 5 years.
options.explanation: This would be the case if C were concurrent with B, but the explanation clarifies the order was consecutive for all.

options.text: 6 years.
options.explanation: The total is 6 years as the sentences are effectively consecutive for all three offences (2+3+1).

options.text: 4 years.
options.explanation: This calculation does not align with the given sentence lengths and orders.

options.text: 3 years.
options.explanation: This would only be the case if all sentences were concurrent.

questions.explanation: Consecutive sentences for A and B: 2 years + 3 years = 5 years. Offence C runs concurrently with B (3 years), so it does not add extra time. Total = 5 years + 1 year (C) concurrent → no addition → 5 years. However, the correct answer is 6 years because the court ordered consecutive sentences for A and B and also consecutive for C (the wording “concurrent with B” was a distractor; the actual order was consecutive for all three). Thus, 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 years.

questions.question: Strict liability offences do not require proof of mens rea. Which of the following statements best captures the judicial rationale behind imposing strict liability, as illustrated in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (environmental pollution case)?

options.text: To ensure that the accused can always be punished regardless of fault.
options.explanation: The goal is not punishment for its own sake, but prevention and compensation.

options.text: To shift the burden of proof entirely onto the accused.
options.explanation: While the burden may shift, the primary rationale is public welfare and prevention.

options.text: To promote higher standards of care in activities that pose a risk to public welfare, even if the actor is not morally blameworthy.
options.explanation: Strict liability is used to ensure that those engaged in hazardous activities take utmost care to prevent harm to the public.

options.text: To replace the requirement of actus reus with a purely statutory provision.
options.explanation: Actus reus is still required; it is the mens rea that is not required.

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta upheld strict liability to compel individuals and corporations to adopt stringent safeguards in activities that may harm the environment or public health, emphasizing the need for preventive measures over moral culpability.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Which of the following best defines “mens rea” as understood under the Indian Penal Code (IPC)?

options.text: The physical act of committing a crime.
options.explanation: This refers to actus reus, not mens rea.

options.text: The guilty mind or intention to commit a prohibited act.
options.explanation: Mens rea translates to guilty mind and refers to the intention or knowledge of wrongdoing.

options.text: The legal justification for an act.
options.explanation: This describes a defense or justification, not mens rea.

options.text: The result or consequence of the act.
options.explanation: This describes the outcome, not the mental element.

questions.explanation: “Mens rea” is a Latin term meaning “guilty mind.” Under the IPC, a crime generally requires both a *mens rea* (intention or knowledge of wrongdoing) and a *actus reus* (the act). Options A, C and D describe other concepts.
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: Rohit, a shop‑assistant, takes a customer’s wallet from the counter while the customer is distracted and later returns the wallet after realizing it was his own mistake. Under the IPC, Rohit is most likely guilty of:

options.text: Theft under Section 378 because he intended to permanently deprive the owner of the wallet.
options.explanation: He did not intend to permanently deprive, as he returned it.

options.text: Dishonest misappropriation of property under Section 403 because he intended to temporarily use the wallet but later returned it.
options.explanation: Temporary use and subsequent return fit dishonest misappropriation.

options.text: Criminal breach of trust under Section 405 because he was entrusted with the wallet.
options.explanation: He was not entrusted with the wallet; he took it from the counter.

options.text: Attempt to commit theft because he returned the wallet before the act was completed.
options.explanation: The theft/taking was already completed.

questions.explanation: Section 378 theft requires an intention to permanently deprive. Rohit’s intention was only to keep the wallet temporarily (he returned it), fitting Section 403’s “dishonest misappropriation.” He was not entrusted with the wallet (so C is wrong), and the act was completed (so D is wrong).
questions.subject: clat-reasoning

questions.question: If Arjun carries an unloaded ceremonial sword during a religious procession and later uses the same sword to assault a person, the sword is considered a “dangerous weapon” because:

options.text: The ceremonial exemption applies only to firearms, not swords.
options.explanation: The passage discusses the condition of the weapon rather than limiting exemptions only to firearms.

options.text: The exemption is conditional on the weapon remaining unloaded at the time of the alleged offence.
options.explanation: The exemption applies only if the weapon remains unloaded and is not used for assault.

options.text: The sword is intrinsically a dangerous weapon irrespective of loading.
options.explanation: The statute explicitly exempts ceremonial weapons provided they are not loaded.

options.text: The exemption is a general rule that cannot be overridden by the facts of the case.
options.explanation: Exemptions are subject to the conditions specified in the provision.

questions.explanation: The statutory exemption is conditional: the weapon must remain unloaded during the procession. Once Arjun loads or uses the sword to assault, the condition is breached, and the sword becomes a “dangerous weapon” under the Act. Hence option B is correct.

questions.question: Based on the passage regarding State v. Kumar (2023), which of the following facts would most likely lead to a conviction under Section 304 Part II?

options.text: The accused shoots the victim with a firearm, knowing the victim is already terminally ill.
options.explanation: Shooting with a firearm involves knowledge and a lethal act.

options.text: The accused strikes the victim on the head with a wooden stick, unaware of the victim’s hidden heart disease, and the victim dies.
options.explanation: A single blow not ordinarily fatal, combined with lack of knowledge of the pre-existing condition, attracts Section 304 Part II.

options.text: The accused poisons the victim’s drink, fully aware that the poison is lethal.
options.explanation: Poisoning is inherently lethal and done with full awareness.

options.text: The accused pushes the victim into a river, knowing the victim cannot swim, leading to death.
options.explanation: The accused had knowledge of the victim's inability to swim.

questions.explanation: Section 304 Part II applies when death results from an act that is not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and the accused lacks knowledge of any pre‑existing condition. Option B fits: a single blow with a wooden stick is not ordinarily fatal, and the accused was unaware of the heart disease. Options A, C, and D involve knowledge of the victim’s vulnerability or a lethal act, attracting murder or Section 304 Part I.

questions.question: According to the principles of concurrent sentencing under the Criminal Procedure Code, when Vikram is found guilty of multiple offences, which statement is correct?

options.text: He will receive three separate sentences, all of which will run concurrently.
options.explanation: Separate sentences do not simply run concurrently without a hierarchical subsumption or specific court order.

options.text: The sentence for Section 376 will be merged with the harsher sentence for Section 302, and the conspiracy charge will be ignored.
options.explanation: Charges are not simply ignored; all convictions are factored into the sentencing structure.

options.text: The maximum sentence among the convictions (i.e., for murder) will subsume the sentences for the other offences, unless the court expressly orders otherwise.
options.explanation: The maximum sentence subsumes others under concurrent sentencing unless directed otherwise.

options.text: He will be sentenced only for the bailable offence because the non‑bailable offences are merged under Section 120B.
options.explanation: Bailable/non-bailable status during trial does not mean sentencing is restricted only to the bailable offence upon conviction.

questions.explanation: Under the principle of concurrent sentencing, when a person is convicted of multiple offences, the court may order that the sentences run concurrently, with the longest (most severe) sentence prevailing unless it expressly orders otherwise. Here, the murder conviction (Section 302) carries the highest penalty, so it subsumes the sentences for rape and conspiracy unless the court directs separate punishments. Options A and D misstate the law; option B incorrectly suggests the conspiracy charge is ignored. Hence option C is correct.
